newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, Germany head for compromise on VW funds.
newsitem.headline: EU, Germany head for compromise on VW funds.

text.p: The European Commission warned Germany on Tuesday that there was no question of Volkswagen AG getting away with subsidies the EU executive has deemed illegal.

But it fell short of saying that some 100 million marks ($68 million) received from the state of Saxony had to be paid back, hinting that the two sides may be heading to one of the European Union's classic, face-saving compromises.
Under an agreement which Bonn must formally endorse, the subsidies would not be repaid but "their effect would be neutralised", an EU source said.
The source would not elaborate, but hinted that some aid previously authorised by the Commission could be cut back to balance the books.
Commission President Jacques Santer also indicated in an interview with news magazine Der Spiegel published on Monday that Saxony should agree to reduce the VW subsidies.

The Commission cleared in late June German aid of 539.1 million marks for VW to help it with investments at its Saxon plants of Mosel and Chemnitz. The manufacturer had initially been promised 779.8 million marks.

But the Saxony government openly challenged the Commission's decision and, according to a Commission official, has already paid over 100 million marks in illegal aid with more pencilled in for 1996 and the next two years.

Santer's spokesman, Nikolaus van der Pas, warned against reading too much in comments by Kurt Biedenkopf, premier of Lower Saxony state, who was reported as saying that the money would not be blocked or handed back.

"Biedenkopf welcomed Santer's offer. He also said there was no question about...giving the money back. Well that's not what the president suggested; if you don't accept that, there is no proposal," van der Pas told the Commission's daily news briefing.
"This blatant illegality must be ended," van der Pas said. "Without this clear condition there will be no solution".
Talks took place all afternoon on Monday between Johannes Ludewig, state secretary at the German Economics Ministry, and Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert.
Commission officials said the ball was now in the German camp with Bonn expected to confirm formally its agreement with the compromise later on Tuesday.
"We expect a reply in written by the German government that Van Miert will take to the Commission meeting tommorrow," one official said.

The Commission has threatened to take Germany to the European court over the payment of illegal subsidies to Volkswagen if its June decision is not respected. The state of Saxony itself has asked the European Court of First Instance, the EU's lower court, to overrule the Commission.

The Volkswagen controversy touches upon the politically sensitive question of massive subsidies to the former east Germany to compensate for decades of communist rule. The Commission believes that enough money has been channeled to the new German states since reunification in 1990, but Saxony claims that it should continue to benefit from special rules.
Sources close to Van Miert said this was not part of the Volkswagen discussion.
